title: Back of the envelope
summary: Storage, bandwidth and the latency numbers every engineer should know in 2026, plus the tools seniors use to check an estimate and to measure the numbers on their own hardware.

steps.title: Storage: rows x size x time x copies
body: Storage grows with every write and almost never shrinks. Estimate it from the **average** write rate:
```text
bytes per day  = average writes/s x bytes per write x 86,400
total          = bytes per day x 365 x years x copies
500 writes/s x 1 KB x 86,400   = 43.2 GB a day
x 365                          = 15.8 TB a year
x 5 years                      = 79 TB
x 3 copies (replication)       = 237 TB
Remember the **copies**: a primary with two replicas, or object storage that keeps data in several zones,
stores every byte more than once. Indexes add more (often 20 to 50% on top of the rows).
Powers of ten are fine for estimates; say which you use. `1 KB = 1,000 bytes` makes the maths easy;
`1 KiB = 1,024 bytes` is what memory and most tools report. The difference is 2.4% per step (7% at GiB vs GB).

steps.prompt: 500 writes per second of 1,000 bytes, kept 5 years, 3 copies. What does this print (in TB)?
steps.explain: 500 x 86,400 x 365 x 5 x 3 x 1,000 bytes = 2.3652 x 10^14 bytes, which is 236.5 TB. In an interview, "about 240 TB" is the right level of precision.

steps.title: Bandwidth: QPS x bytes x 8
body: Network links are sold in **bits** per second; payloads are measured in **bytes**. Multiply by 8.
```text
egress bits/s = peak QPS x response bytes x 8
20,000 QPS x 50 KB x 8 = 8 Gbit/s
Then compare with what you have. A common cloud instance has a 10 to 25 Gbit/s network card, often less
for small sizes, and big instances go to 100 Gbit/s or more. Internet egress is usually billed per GB,
so at high volume bandwidth can cost more than the servers. That is a big reason for CDNs and compression.

prompt: **Load-test report.** An image service sends 4,000 responses per second at peak, average 300 KB each,
from 4 small servers with a 2.5 Gbit/s network card each, evenly balanced. CPU is at 35%, yet p99 latency
is climbing and the load tester reports timeouts. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The network cards: 4,000 x 300 KB x 8 = 9.6 Gbit/s, so each card carries 2.4 of its 2.5 Gbit/s
The CPU: 35% is too high for an image service
The load balancer algorithm: round robin causes timeouts
Not enough memory: images should be cached
explain: Do the sum: 4,000 x 300,000 x 8 = 9.6 Gbit/s; over 4 cards that is 2.4 Gbit/s each, 96% of the card.
Packets queue in the network stack, so latency climbs while CPU looks idle. Fixes: bigger instances
(more bandwidth per card), more servers, a CDN in front, or smaller images (modern formats, resizing).
A 30-second sum finds this before anyone starts profiling the code.

steps.title: Numbers every engineer should know (2026)
body: Orders of magnitude, not exact values. Hardware varies; measure your own (the toolkit shows how).
| Operation | Typical time |
| L1 cache reference | about 1 ns |
| Main memory reference | about 100 ns |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from memory | tens of microseconds |
| NVMe SSD random 4 KB read | 20 to 100 microseconds |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from NVMe | about 0.2 ms |
| Round trip in the same availability zone | 0.1 to 0.5 ms |
| Round trip between zones in one region | 0.5 to 2 ms |
| Hard disk seek | 5 to 10 ms |
| Round trip US East to EU West | about 70 to 80 ms |
| Round trip across the Pacific | 100 to 200 ms |
What follows from them:
- Memory is about **1,000 times** faster than a random SSD read: hot data belongs in RAM (caches).
- A same-zone network hop costs about as much as several SSD reads: chatty services (10 calls per request) add up.
- Light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond. No design makes London to Sydney faster than about 250 ms
round trip: put data near users instead.

steps.prompt: Match each operation to its order of magnitude.
pairs: Round trip in the same zone
Round trip US East to EU West
steps.explain: Each step is roughly ten times the one before. Knowing the ladder lets you spot a design that does a cross-region call inside a loop.

steps.prompt: Order these from fastest to slowest.
lines: Round trip between two zones of one region
Round trip US East to EU West
steps.explain: 1 ns, 100 ns, about 50 us, about 1 ms, about 75 ms. Each jump is at least ten times.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: checking an estimate
steps.body: Seniors do the arithmetic in a shell, out loud, and then measure the real numbers on the hardware they will run on.

toolkit.what: A calculator that is always there. Underscores in numbers keep the zeros readable.
flags: run one line of Python and exit
toolkit.when: turning DAU into peak QPS during a design review

toolkit.what: Turns a long byte count into 237T (powers of 1,000) or 216Ti (powers of 1,024), so you can read it.
flags: K, M, G, T as powers of 1,000
Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti as powers of 1,024

toolkit.what: Arbitrary precision arithmetic with a maths library, for when integer shell arithmetic truncates.
flags: load the maths library and use 20 decimal places

toolkit.what: Measures what a disk really does: random reads, writes, latency percentiles and IOPS.
flags: random reads (also read, write, randwrite, randrw)
bypass the page cache, or you measure RAM
toolkit.when: before trusting a vendor's IOPS number for a database volume

toolkit.what: Measures network throughput between two hosts (run `iperf3 -s` on one first).
flags: be the client and connect to host

toolkit.what: Round-trip time between two hosts: the zone and region numbers above, measured.

steps.prompt: Measure 4 KB **random reads** on a new database volume, without the page cache flattering the result.
steps.explain: `randread` with `--bs=4k` matches a database's random page reads. `--direct=1` bypasses the page cache; without it you measure RAM and the number looks wonderful.

steps.title: An estimate calculator
prompt: Write two methods for the estimates you just did by hand (use `double` arithmetic, 1 TB = 10^12 bytes,
- `double StorageTb(double writesPerSec, double bytesPerWrite, double years, int copies)`: total storage in TB.
- `double Gbps(double qps, double bytesPerResponse)`: egress in Gbit/s. `Gbps(20000, 50000)` is `8`.
starter: double StorageTb(double writesPerSec, double bytesPerWrite, double years, int copies)
solution: double StorageTb(double writesPerSec, double bytesPerWrite, double years, int copies)
var bytes = writesPerSec * bytesPerWrite * 86_400 * 365 * years * copies;
hints: Bits are bytes times 8; divide by `1e9` for Gbit/s and by `1e12` for TB.
template: Dojo.Eq("500 writes/s, 1 KB, 5 years, 3 copies", 236.52, Math.Round(StorageTb(500, 1000, 5, 3), 2));
Dojo.Eq("100 writes/s, 2 KB, 1 year, 1 copy", 6.31, Math.Round(StorageTb(100, 2000, 1, 1), 2));
